summary:
Emberlog is a live web app that turns 26 years of NASA satellite fire data into one consistent record for Pakistan and India, and uses it to forecast next week’s burning.
NASA has tracked fires with MODIS since 2000 and the sharper VIIRS since 2012, but VIIRS detects about 5.5 times more fires. Compared directly, burning appears to explode in 2012 simply because the sensor changed. We processed 8.5 million NASA FIRMS detections into 5,381 boxes of 25 km per week, and trained a LightGBM model on the years when both satellites overlapped to learn what VIIRS would have seen. Applied to 2000–2011, it produces one harmonized record that beat simple ratio scaling on every test measure for unseen 2024–2025 data.
On top of this record, Emberlog shows a burning calendar for any area (seasons, unusual weeks, long-term trends) and forecasts next week’s fire risk per box (ROC-AUC 0.91), with plain-English SHAP explanations and wind-based smoke warnings.
This matters because crop burning in Punjab drives the winter smog that shuts schools in Lahore and Delhi. A consistent record shows whether burning is truly changing, and early warnings give agencies time to act.
details:
What it does and how it works

Emberlog turns 26 years of NASA satellite fire data into one consistent record for Pakistan and India, then uses it to forecast and explain next week’s burning.

  1. Data: We processed 8.5 million NASA FIRMS active-fire detections (MODIS 2000–2025, VIIRS S-NPP 2012–2025), kept vegetation fires only, and counted them per week in 5,381 boxes of about 25 km.
  2. Harmonization: VIIRS detects about 5.5 times more fires than MODIS, so raw records show a false jump in 2012. A LightGBM model learned, from the years when both satellites overlapped, how many fires VIIRS would have seen given MODIS. A second model covers 2000–2002, when only the Terra satellite flew. Applied to 2000–2011, they create one continuous VIIRS-equivalent record. On unseen 2024–2025 data the model beat simple ratio scaling on every measure, with 22% less error per box.
  3. Burning calendar: For any area, it shows a 26-year week-by-year heatmap, the main burning seasons, unusually heavy or quiet weeks, and the long-term trend.
  4. Forecast: A second LightGBM model predicts each box’s chance of fire next week from recent fires, neighbouring boxes, last year, and the 5-year seasonal pattern. On unseen data it reached ROC-AUC 0.91 and caught 77% of fires, beating “repeat this week” (0.78) and the “five-year average” (0.86).
  5. Explanations and smoke: SHAP values become plain sentences explaining each box’s risk, and Meteomatics wind data estimates whether smoke will drift toward cities such as Lahore or Delhi.

Benefits and intended impact

Punjab’s crop-stubble burning drives the winter smog that closes schools in Lahore and Delhi. Emberlog gives agencies and policymakers a fair long-term record to judge whether burning is really rising or falling, plus a week of warning to act before peak weeks: targeting enforcement, offering alternatives to farmers, and preparing hospitals. Researchers and journalists get consistent data, and citizens can see when smoke is heading their way. The method works anywhere the same open NASA data exists.

Tools and technologies

  • Data and ML: Python, pandas, NumPy, LightGBM, SHAP (TreeSHAP), scikit-learn, Matplotlib
  • Backend: FastAPI and Uvicorn, with memory-mapped NumPy arrays
  • Frontend: React, Vite, Leaflet, Recharts
  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP 375 m), NASA Black Marble via GIBS, Meteomatics Weather API, Esri basemap
  • Deployment: Docker, Railway, GitHub, with auto-deploy on every push

No special hardware: everything was built and trained on our laptops.

What makes it creative

  • It treats harmonization as a learning problem, not a fixed conversion factor, and proves the model beats the simple approach.
  • It turns the harmonized record into action: a forecast rather than just a historical chart.
  • Every prediction explains itself in plain language, so non-experts can trust and question it.
  • It links fire forecasts to wind to show where smoke will go, connecting satellite data to the smog people actually breathe.
  • A night-satellite map with glowing fire boxes makes the data easy to grasp at a glance.

Factors we considered

  • Fair testing: we trained on 2012–2021, tuned on 2022–2023, and tested on 2024–2025, which the models never saw. The forecast uses only past information, so no future data leaks in.
  • Baselines: every model is compared against simple methods, to prove the ML is worth it.
  • Satellite differences: we treated the Terra-only years (2000–2002) separately and marked them as lower confidence.
  • Honesty about limits: the model over-predicted autumn 2024, when burning suddenly fell, likely because of enforcement. Satellites also miss fires lit after they pass overhead. We say this openly in the app.
  • Accessibility and cost: plain-English explanations, a mobile-friendly design, and a backend slimmed to run on free hosting.
